Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(d\in\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250\}\) and write \(x_d=\max A_d\).

Because \(|A_d|=d\), we have \(x_d\ge d\). Also, for any two indices \(d,e\), the set \(A_d\cup A_e\) contains \(d+e-\gcd(d,e)\) distinct positive integers, so
\[
\max(x_d,x_e)\ge d+e-\gcd(d,e).
\]
This gives a small linear-programming problem. In particular, the optimal values are forced to be
\[
x_1\ge 1,\quad x_2\ge 2,\quad x_5\ge 6,\quad x_{10}\ge 10,\quad x_{25}\ge 30,
\]
\[
x_{50}\ge 50,\quad x_{125}\ge 150,\quad x_{250}\ge 250.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
\ge 1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

This lower bound is attainable. For example, take
\[
A_1=\{1\},\; A_2=\{1,2\},\; A_5=\{1,3,4,5,6\},\; A_{10}=\{1,2,\dots,10\},
\]
\[
A_{25}=A_5\cup\{11,12,\dots,30\},\;
A_{50}=\{1,2,\dots,50\},
\]
\[
A_{125}=A_{25}\cup\{51,52,\dots,150\},\;
A_{250}=\{1,2,\dots,250\}.
\]
One checks that the pairwise intersection sizes are \(\gcd(i,j)\), and the maxima are exactly
\[
1,2,6,10,30,50,150,250,
\]
so the sum is \(499\). Hence the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
